title: LRU warmup anomaly dive
content:
Summary:
This is a working note capturing an investigation into an LRU warmup anomaly we observed on the 4-GPU p4d-like clusters. Symptoms: after starting a service or following an autoscale event, TTL-warmup and LRU warming behaved suboptimally — reuse rates took longer than expected to converge and memory bandwidth spiked briefly, causing tail latency regressions on small-request workloads.

Why this matters:
- Higher-than-expected paging/eviction churn increases token cost and tail latency.
- Cold-warm transitions impact canary rollouts (we saw canary failures due to latency SLO misses).

Observed behavior (empirical):
- Warmup window ~30-90s where reuse rate climbs slowly (expected <20s).
- Short spikes in device memory bandwidth measured at ~72-84 GB/s sustained for 5-15s on p4d (baseline sustained for same workload usually 40-50 GB/s).
- KV hit rate ramped from 12% -> 55% over 90s instead of 12% -> 75% in previous stable runs.
- Eviction counts per-sec increased 3.2x during warmup window.

Reproduction notes (how to reproduce locally / cluster):
- Start the inference worker with the same model variant and cache-size=8GB on a p4d-8x.
- Load test using bench-client with 8 concurrent clients issuing short prompts (avg tokens/request ~36) at 200 QPS for 3 minutes.
- Command snippet (bench):
  ./bench-client --target=https://svc.local:8443/generate --conns=8 --qps=200 --prompt-set=short-prompts.json --duration=180
- Use the runtime flags: --kv-cache-size=8G --eviction-policy=lru --kv-prefetch=off --kv-warmup=on

What we profiled:
- CPU sampling (perf) on worker main loop (focus on cache manager, page fault handler)
- GPU device memory copy counters and nvprof traces for memcpy patterns during warmup
- Runtime internal metrics: kv_hits, kv_misses, kv_evictions, kv_prefetches, kv_warmup_progress, kv_warmup_iterations
- OS-level metrics: minor/major page faults, RSS, anon memory scanning

Key low-level findings:
1) Eviction thrash on initial load path
   - The cache manager was aggressively evicting entries created during the first 10s because of a conservative LRU timestamp aging routine. We observed many entries with near-identical access timestamps due to the batch prefetch pattern, which confused the eviction ranking and caused oscillation: A gets evicted, later re-inserted, then evicted again.

2) Prefetch/backfill pattern created write-amplification across memory regions
   - When warmup was enabled, the background backfill thread enqueued large sequential insert operations. The insert order caused hotset items to be interleaved with cold items; because LRU aging uses access-time micro-buckets updated only on access, insertion time ordering created a false cold classification for some hot entries.

3) Memory bandwidth spikes correlate with large fragmented memcpy (CPU -> device) bursts, not with sustained token decoding
   - nvprof and device counters show that memcpy_large (chunks of 4-16MB) originated from backfill path. These bursts align with higher eviction counts (we suspect thrash causes repeated read+rewrite cycles of the same keys).

4) Prefetch off path performed better in our microbench but exposed higher tail latency during heavy concurrent loads
   - Turning off kv-prefetch reduced bandwidth spikes but slowed overall hit-rate ramp; there is a trade-off between interrupting steady-state serving and micro-optimizing warmup.

Hypotheses (ranked):
- H1: LRU aging granularity is too coarse; simultaneous batch accesses produce identical timestamps so LRU ties are broken by insertion order causing evictions of useful items.
- H2: Backfill/insertion ordering lacks hotness signal. Without an access-based boost, new hot items get placed low in the recency stack.
- H3: Eviction policy doesn't consider size/weight (single-entry granularity) causing large entries to evict many small hot entries (weight-aware eviction could help).
- H4: Page-level fragmentation on the worker's allocator exacerbates device memcpy patterns, raising observed memory bandwidth during warmup.

Quick experiments and results (notes):
- Exp A: Add micro-bucketed timestamping (32ms buckets) to break ties and prefer recently accessed over merely inserted entries. Result: warmup ramp shortened by ~22% in 3/4 runs, evictions down by ~18%.
- Exp B: Change backfill to insert hotset-first using a tiny LRU sampling pass immediately after load. Result: hit-rate ramp improved to 70% at 60s, but initial latency some times spiked due to short-term write stalls.
- Exp C: Switch to size-weighted eviction (evict by smallest benefit-first). Result: mixed — helped when workload had many small frequent KV entries, but worsened tail when large value entries were genuinely cold but took time to rehydrate.
- Exp D: Limit backfill memcpy chunk-size to 256KB and make it rate-limited. Result: memory bandwidth spikes reduced 40% and tail latencies improved; however warmup longer by ~10% vs bucketed-timestamps approach.

Profiling snippets (representative):
- perf top samples: cache_manager::evict_loop 31%, cache_manager::insert_path 18%, memcopy_worker 12%, page_fault_handler 7%
- nvprof traces: memcpy_sync large_chunk at t=13s, 22s, 37s (aligns with eviction spikes)
- runtime metrics (sampled second-by-second):
  t=0s: hits=0, misses=200/s, evictions=0
  t=15s: hits=8%, evictions=72/s
  t=45s: hits=41%, evictions=20/s
  t=90s: hits=63%, evictions=6/s

Open questions / unknowns:
- Does allocator fragmentation affect memcpy pattern significantly across different instance types (p4d vs a100p)? Need cross-instance runs.
- How much of the problem is specific to our LRU implementation vs general to any single-list recency structure?
- Could KV TTL heuristics (recently-created items get TTL grace) reduce thrash without hurting steady-state?

Next actions (concrete):
1) Run Exp A + D combined (bucketed timestamp + smaller memcpy chunks + rate limit), 6-run batch across p4d and a100p for statistical significance. Owner: Miguel. Target by 2025-02-05.
2) Add micro-bench that produces deterministic access skew and measure weighted-eviction tradeoffs. Owner: Connor. Target by 2025-01-25.
3) PoC a hotset-first backfill using a sampling pass; measure insert stall characteristics and add non-blocking insert mode. Owner: Sofia. Target by 2025-02-12.
4) Postmortem note for the canary incident (timestamps + logs) and link to this doc. Owner: Aisha. Target: 2025-01-20.

Notes to self / rough todo checklist:
- [ ] Add unit tests for timestamp bucket logic
- [ ] Expose cheap metric: "kv_reinsert_rate" to detect thrash earlier
- [ ] Add a runtime flag to cap memcpy chunk size for quick experiments
- [ ] Schedule cross-instance runs with infra (request p4d and a100 reserved slots)

Appendix (raw log exerpt):
- 2025-01-12T13:02:11Z INFO kv: insert key=0x7f4b size=1200 ts=170
actions=backfill
- 2025-01-12T13:02:12Z WARN kv: evict key=0x7f4b winner=key=0x6a12 reason=age_tie
- 2025-01-12T13:02:13Z INFO memcopy: started chunk=0 len=8388608 src=heap dst=device

If you pick this up: start with Exp A+D combined and instrument: kv_reinsert_rate, kv_warmup_iterations, and add an event sample that records (key, age_bucket, insert_rank) for 1% of events to reason about ordering.
